tasks.task: Read the brief and clarify the scope
tasks.what: Understand the client's expectations, the scope, the timeline and which optional modules are expected, before any work starts.
tasks.how:
Read the brief and create a working sheet listing: client and business question, category in scope, markets (countries), languages, period, platforms, deliverable format and due date.
Clarify the optional modules, one by one, and write a yes / no for each:; (1) Ratings & reviews (R&R): required or not, and propose which e-retailers would best fit.; (2) Brand focus: is the audit run for a specific brand? If yes, a Brand zoom-in section is needed (phase 8).; (3) Competitive landscape: market / cultural context, territories mapping, purchase destinations.; (4) Personas: overview only, or overview + one ID card per persona.; (5) Benchmark category (see 0.3).; (6) Competitors to benchmark in the brand zoom-in, if the client named them.
Clarify the category perimeter at a high level: which sub-categories and product types are in, which are out (detailed in 1.1).
Validate the list above with the project lead.
Done when: every scope item and every optional module has a validated yes / no, written in the working sheet.
tasks.watch_out:
Anything left implicit in the brief (e.g. "premium", "prestige", "body care") must be turned into an explicit perimeter: it drives the query, the volume and the brand clusters.
If the brief mixes a category audit and a brand audit, agree which one leads the storyline: the category audit structure stays the backbone, the brand appears in the Brand zoom-in.
tasks.output: Validated scope, list of optional modules (yes / no)

tasks.task: Check previous Semantiweb work that overlaps with the brief
tasks.what: Reuse what has already been delivered so the audit starts from existing knowledge, has a reference point, and stays consistent with past numbers.
tasks.how:
Ask the project lead and the analyst channels on Slack for any past project that overlaps with the current brief: same category, same country with a similar category (e.g. skincare for a makeup brief), or a brand audit where this category was covered for the same scope.
For each project found, note in the working sheet: name, period covered, markets, platforms, and what can be reused (desk research, queries, facets, brand lists and clusters, volumes, personas, territories).
Keep the volumes and evolutions of these projects: they are the reference for the proportion check in 3.5.
Done when: the list of overlapping projects (or "none found") is in the working sheet and validated by the project lead.
tasks.watch_out:
Past work for another client can be used internally as a methodological starting point (queries, facet logic, vocabulary). Never show another client's results, verbatims or brand-specific findings in this deliverable, and never name another client.
Note the time gap with each past project: a large gap means volumes and brand rankings must be rebuilt, not copied.
tasks.output: List of overlapping projects with reusable elements and their volumes

tasks.task: Decide whether a benchmark is needed, and which one
tasks.what: Give the client a point of comparison so the category's numbers can be read (is +2% growth or 39% positivity high or low?).
tasks.how:
Ask the project lead whether the brief expects a benchmark. If yes, pick an adjacent category that consumers and the client would see as relevant: e.g. for a makeup category audit, the benchmark can be beauty overall or skincare; for prestige haircare, the benchmark can be total haircare or beauty.
Agree on which KPIs will be benchmarked (typically: volume and evolution, platform split, sentiment, top topics) and keep the same period, markets and platforms as the main category.
If R&R is in scope, the category average is itself the benchmark for each product KPI (rating, recommendation rate, sampling rate, etc., see phase 9).
Done when: the benchmark (or "no benchmark") and its KPIs are validated and logged.
tasks.watch_out: A benchmark needs its own query and volume check (3.2): plan the time for it in the staffing.
tasks.output: Benchmark decision and KPI list in the decision log

tasks.what: Make sure the right number of analysts and hours is planned to deliver on time.
tasks.how:
From the deliverable structure (which sections and optional modules are in scope, see Deck Structure tab), the timeline and the number of analysts available, estimate the man-hours needed per phase.
Check the staffing on Float and adjust it with the project lead (who does what, who covers which section).
Done when: staffing is validated on Float by the project lead.
tasks.watch_out: Optional modules weigh a lot: personas with ID cards, a brand zoom-in and R&R can each add several days. Count them explicitly.

tasks.task: Open the working sheet and the decision log
tasks.what: Have one place where every scope decision, source and number is traceable.
tasks.how:
Working sheet (Project Drive): one section per phase (scope, perimeter, brand list and clusters, viral launches, hashtags, volumes per tool, facets, frequencies, verbatim candidates).
Decision log (Project Drive): one line per decision with date and who decided (e.g. "body cleansers excluded", "benchmark = skincare", "spike of March excluded", "Brand X moved from Indie to Prestige").
Done when: both files exist in the Project Drive and are shared with the team.
tasks.watch_out: Log every perimeter and cluster decision: it is what you rely on when the client questions a number.

tasks.what: Write down exactly which product formats belong to the category, so the query, the facets and the volumes all measure the same thing.
tasks.how:
List the sub-categories and, for each one, the product types it contains. Example (body care): body cream, body lotion, body serum, body oil are IN; body cleanser / shower gel are OUT. Example (prestige haircare): Cleanse (shampoo, dry shampoo), Care (conditioner, mask, oil, serum, leave-in), Styling (sprays, creams, gels, mousses).
Define the price / positioning level when the brief names one ("premium", "prestige", "mass"): it decides which brands enter the query; ask if the client has given specific brand clusters.
Note borderline products and the decision taken for each (e.g. hair tools, hair supplements, hair & body mists).
Validate the perimeter with the project lead.
Done when: the perimeter table (sub-category / product types in / product types out) is validated and logged.
tasks.watch_out: Borderline products are where volumes go wrong: one generic product word (e.g. "mask", "oil", "serum") can pull in another category. Flag them now, they will need context words in the query (3.1).
tasks.output: Validated perimeter table in the working sheet

tasks.task: Desk research on the market in each country
tasks.what: Understand how the category works in each market in scope, to explain the data later and to build the market context slide.
tasks.how:
Read articles, market reports and retailer pages on the category in each country: size and growth, key players, local champions vs international brands, distribution channels (salons, prestige retailers, pharmacy, e-commerce, discounters), price levels.
Scroll the platforms in scope with the main category hashtags (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, local forums) to see how consumers talk about it: vocabulary, content formats (GRWM, tutorials, before / after, hauls, reviews), types of creators (professionals, experts, educators, influencers).
Note cultural specifics that will frame the reading: aesthetic codes, who consumers trust (professionals, peers, apps such as Yuka / INCI Beauty), identity topics, regulation or scrutiny on ingredients, cultural practices/moments.
Save every source link in the working sheet.
Done when: a short market note per country (key players, channels, trust structure, cultural codes) with sources is in the working sheet.
tasks.watch_out: Claude can be used as a cross-check, not as a source: keep a link for every fact. Have local vocabulary checked by a native speaker.
tasks.output: Market note per country with sources

tasks.task: Build the brand list and the brand clusters
tasks.what: Know which brands make up the category and group them into clusters that follow the market's competitive logic.
tasks.how:
List all relevant brands of the category in each market (from desk research, retailer assortments, past projects found in 0.2).
Group them into brand clusters. Define each cluster on 3 criteria: pricing, distribution, purchase driver. Example (prestige haircare): PRESTIGE (premium to very high price; Sephora, department stores, brands.com; heritage, sensorial experience, science-backed claims), SALON & PRO (mid to premium; hair salons first; hairstylist recommendation and technical authority), INDIE (mid to premium-accessible; Sephora, DTC, social commerce; social-led discovery, founder story, need-specific claims).
Flag local brands (e.g. Indian brands in a India audit) so they can be marked on the slides.
Validate the clusters with the project lead; if the client has its own segmentation, use it or log why not.
Done when: brand list with one cluster per brand and the cluster definitions are validated. This feeds the Lexicon slide, the brand segmentation facet and the query.
tasks.watch_out:
A brand must sit in one cluster only. Borderline brands (e.g. a salon brand now sold at Sephora): decide and log.
Keep 3 to 4 clusters maximum: more clusters make the SOV splits unreadable.
tasks.output: Brand list, cluster definitions (Lexicon), decision log entries

tasks.task: List recent viral launches and key moments
tasks.what: Know which launches, products and events drove conversation over the period, to explain peaks and rising words.
tasks.how:
For the main brands of each cluster, list launches and moments over the period (L24M): new products and ranges, launches that went viral on TikTok / Instagram, collabs, celebrity brands entering the category, retailer events (Black Friday, Prime Day), trends (e.g. glass hair, slicked bun, skinification).
Note for each: date, brand, product, type of moment, link.
Done when: the list is in the working sheet with links.
tasks.watch_out: These product and trend names must also go into the query (3.1) and the facets (4.1), otherwise their conversation is missed.
tasks.output: Launch & moments list in the working sheet

tasks.what: Avoid launching crawls that the scope does not need.
tasks.how:
Ask the project lead which of the steps 2.1 to 2.4 are needed for this audit (TikTok hashtag crawl, Reddit crawl, TikTok comment export, e-commerce reviews).
Launch the needed crawls on day 1 of the project: they can take up to 2 working days.
Done when: the list of crawls to run is validated.
tasks.watch_out: Crawls are the longest lead time of the project: do not wait for the query to be final.

tasks.what: Crawl TikTok content on the category with the Semantiweb crawlers.
tasks.how:
Identify 30 to 50 consumer hashtags that are (1) relevant to the category and (2) exclusive to it (e.g. #cheveuxabimes, #hairroutine, #curlyhairroutine for haircare; avoid generic ones such as #beauty or #selfcare that pull in other categories).
Include sub-category and need hashtags, local-language hashtags, and the key trend hashtags found in 1.4.
Corpus Manager ([internal link] > Sources / crawls > TikTok crawler ([internal link] > NEW PROJECT: one project for the category (plus one for the brand if a brand zoom-in is in scope).
Check that the request appears in Slack #notif-corpus-manager-crawls and follow its progress.
Done when: the crawl output is received and readable.
tasks.watch_out: If the crawl is not finished after 2 working days, contact the Tech team on Slack.

tasks.what: Crawl Reddit data on the category with the Semantiweb crawlers.
tasks.how:
Select the subreddits linked to the category, its sub-categories and its main brands (local subreddits first for a single-country audit).
Corpus Manager > Sources / crawls > Reddit crawler ([internal link] > NEW PROJECT: one project for the category (plus one for the brand if needed).
Check that the request appears in Slack #notif-corpus-manager-crawls and follow its progress.
Done when: the crawl output is received and readable.
tasks.watch_out: If the crawl is not finished after 2 working days, contact the Tech team on Slack.

tasks.what: Collect the comments of the most commented category videos with Export Comments.
tasks.how:
Check that the "Sorter For TikTok & Instagram" extension is installed on your computer.
On TikTok, search the category terms / main sub-categories > Videos tab > sort by comments, descending > scroll down 10 times to refresh the data.
In the working sheet, list the 50 most commented videos: one column for the link, one for the number of comments.
In Export Comments, paste the video links and launch the export.
Done when: the comment export is received.
tasks.watch_out: Comments are where peer advice and questions live (e.g. "is this suitable for wavy hair?"): they matter for topics and personas.

tasks.task: Collect e-commerce reviews (if R&R in scope)
tasks.what: Collect e-commerce reviews for the ratings & reviews analysis.
tasks.how:
List the products to analyze: the client's hero products and the competitor product each one is compared with, plus the products needed to compute the category average.
Check that they are in the Semantiweb reviews database: ICC > R&R - Semantiweb reviews Live Deduplicate.
If not, email the R&R crawl owner the products to crawl and the e-retailer scope (e.g. Sephora, as stated in the brief).
Done when: all products are available in the reviews database.
tasks.watch_out: If you are unsure about the e-retailer scope, validate it with the project lead. If the crawl is not finished after 2 working days, contact the Tech team on Slack.
tasks.output: Products available in the reviews database

tasks.what: Build the extraction query in Radarly that captures the whole category conversation, and only it.
tasks.how:
Content of the query: (1) all mentions of the category as a whole (e.g. haircare, soin cheveux, soin capillaire); (2) every product type within the perimeter (1.1), in every language in scope, with singular / plural and spelling variants; (3) brand names of the brand list (1.3) combined with category words when the brand also sells outside the category; (4) key product, range and trend names from 1.4; (5) the consumer hashtags from 2.1.
Exclusions: products outside the perimeter (e.g. body cleanser for a body care audit), homonyms, brand-owned accounts and official retailers when the brief is consumer-only, giveaways and contests, job offers, bots.
Use context words (AND / NEAR) for generic product words that exist in other categories (e.g. "mask" AND hair words).
Build it in Radarly > New query with the Claude skill "building radarly queries".
Check quality on the RANDOM display of posts (not top posts): read, spot noise, add exclusions, repeat.
Attach the final query to the working sheet. Reference: sample category query [TO ATTACH].
Done when: random reading shows mostly relevant posts and the project lead validates the query.
tasks.watch_out:
Radarly character / term limits: split into several queries (e.g. one per sub-category) and check they do not overlap.
A spike from a single news or celebrity event ( especially from X): validate with project lead/analyst if include, exclude or cap the period and log it.
tasks.output: Validated category query in Radarly, attached to the working sheet

tasks.task: Build the brand and benchmark queries (if in scope)
tasks.what: Get the extraction queries needed for the Brand zoom-in and the benchmark.
tasks.how:
Brand zoom-in: build the brand query following the Brand Audit methodology (step 3.1: brand name and variants, products, key hashtags, ambassadors, exclusions), restricted to the category perimeter.
Competitors named by the client: same logic, one query per competitor, or reuse the queries of past audits (0.2) if the time gap is small.
Benchmark category (0.3): build a lighter query with the same platforms, markets and period.
Done when: each query is validated on the random display by the project lead.
tasks.watch_out: The brand query must be consistent with the category query: every brand post counted in the zoom-in should also be in the category corpus.

tasks.task: Get the volume and cross-check it in Talkwalker and Meltwater
tasks.what: Check volume, evolution and platform split in tools that do not crawl, so the numbers are available quickly.
tasks.how:
Radarly: log the category volume per platform, per month, per market.
Talkwalker > Topic Analytics > build or select the category topic > filters: Consumer voice + country + 2Y data > log volume and evolution by platform in the working sheet.
Meltwater: ask the Meltwater account owner on Slack for access > log volume and evolution by platform, especially TikTok.
Done when: volumes and evolutions per platform from the 3 tools are side by side in the working sheet.
tasks.watch_out: In Talkwalker, check that no other brands or topics are pre-selected; deselect them if they are.
tasks.output: Volumes by platform per tool in the working sheet

tasks.what: If TikTok needs more volume than Meltwater gives, log the Spate and Visibrain volumes.
tasks.how:
Spate: Trends and/or Brands sections > enter the category hashtags (e.g. #haircare: number of posts) > log the volumes in the working sheet.
Visibrain: get your own access and follow the Visibrain guide to build a query.
Done when: TikTok volumes from the additional tools are logged.
tasks.watch_out: Ask your project lead for the Spate access. Never copy logins into shared documents.
tasks.output: Spate / Visibrain volumes in the working sheet

tasks.task: Check that volumes are in proportion with previous work
tasks.what: Make sure the volume is consistent with what Semantiweb already delivered to this client and on this or similar categories.
tasks.how:
Compare the volume and the platform split with the projects found in 0.2: same client, same category, similar categories, brand audits covering the category.
Ratios to check: category volume vs previous category volume (same period length), brand volume vs category volume (share of the brand in its category), platform split.
If a ratio looks off (e.g. the brand weighs more than its category, a platform doubled without explanation), look for the cause: query too narrow / too broad, missing viral topic, noise, perimeter change. Fix or document.
Done when: each gap is either fixed or explained in the working sheet.
tasks.watch_out: A large gap between tools or with past work usually signals a query issue: are we missing a viral topic or a sub-category?

tasks.what: Send the project lead a recommendation for the final volume and wait for approval.
tasks.how:
One recommendation per platform: Instagram normally from Radarly or Meltwater, Reddit from Radarly or Meltwater, TikTok from Meltwater (or crawl + Spate).
Fact-check the evolutions (L12M vs P12M) with Talkwalker.
Send the recommendation with the proportion check (3.5) attached.
Done when: the project lead approves the final volume.
tasks.watch_out: Do not start corpus construction before approval: a volume change afterwards means rebuilding the corpus.
tasks.output: Final volume validated by the project lead

tasks.what: Decide which facets the corpus needs, so every slide of the deck can be computed from it.
tasks.how:
Start from the deliverable structure (Deck Structure tab) and the scope: each slide needs one or several facets.
Standard category facets (see Facets tab for definitions and examples): sub-categories; time frame (L12M vs P12M); seasons; brand segmentation (clusters) and top brands; basic indicators (platform, market, sentiment); drivers; positive attributes; negative attributes; benefits / results expected; concerns (skin or hair concerns); skin types / hair types; body zones (when relevant); ingredients; textures; scents; formats; routines & gestures; occasions; weather; ages / audiences.
Add the module facets when in scope: territories (5.6), purchase destinations (5.5), personas (phase 7), brand values (8.4), content formats.
Fill each facet with the vocabulary from desk research (1.2), the brand list (1.3) and the launches (1.4), in every language in scope. Use the Claude skill "building corpus facets" and ask in Slack #analysts for an existing facet set on the same or a similar category.
Done when: the facet list with vocabulary is validated by the project lead.
tasks.watch_out: A facet that no slide uses is wasted time; a slide without its facet is a blocker later. Map facets to slides before building.

tasks.what: Build the category corpus in Corpus Manager, following the same process as the brand audit.; If a brand zoom-in is in scope; include the brand extracts within the category corpus, make sure there is a facette to isolate the brand's conversations.
tasks.how:
Once the project lead has validated the volume (3.6), run the Radarly / Meltwater extracts and load them into Corpus Manager.
Load the Meltwater TikTok extracts, the TikTok hashtag crawls, the Reddit crawls and the Export Comments data.
Request or run the deduplication, translate if translation is needed (validate with project lead).
Apply the facets defined in 4.1.
Done when: the corpus is deduplicated and all facets are applied.
tasks.watch_out: If R&R is in scope, build a separate reviews corpus (different facets and displays, see 4.4).
tasks.tools: Radarly, Meltwater, Corpus Manager, Export Comments

tasks.task: Build the reviews corpus (if R&R in scope)
tasks.what: Build the R&R corpus for hero product assessment.
tasks.how:
Load the reviews of the products listed in 2.4 into a separate corpus.
Facets: product, brand, rating, sentiment, advantages, disadvantages, recommendation, repurchase intention, sampling (incentivized / free product), period.
Done when: reviews corpus is ready and the category averages can be computed.
tasks.watch_out: Do not mix reviews with social posts in the same corpus.

tasks.task: Validate the corpus and the facets
tasks.what: Check that the corpus is clean and that every facet captures what it should.
tasks.how:
Read posts on the random display, per platform and per market; depollute (add exclusions, remove noise sources).
For each facet: check the distribution (empty values, one value taking almost everything) and read a sample of posts tagged with each main value to check precision.
Fix the facet vocabulary where needed and re-apply.
Done when: the project lead validates the corpus and the facet distributions.
tasks.watch_out: Generic words (e.g. "dry" for hair and skin, "oil" as ingredient and as product) cause most false tags: check them first.

tasks.what: As soon as the corpus is ready, run the word and hashtag frequencies needed for the rising words, sentiment drivers and personas.
tasks.how:
In the corpus, select the facets (market, timeline, sub-category, brand cluster).
Run the frequencies in "Lexical & Hashtags" on L12M and P12M, at total category level and per sub-category and cluster.
Done when: frequency exports are saved in the Project Drive.

tasks.what: Show the size, evolution and structure of the category conversation.
tasks.how:
Total mentions over the period (e.g. 47K) and evolution L12M vs P12M in %.
Share of positive sentiment and its evolution in pts (headline only, detail in 5.3).
Split by platform (% of conversation volume) with the evolution of each platform in pts.
Split by sub-category (% base 100) with evolution in pts (e.g. Cleanse 49% -6 pts, Care 46% +3 pts, Styling 6% +3 pts).
Explain the dynamics in the headline bullets: which platform drives or brakes growth, which sub-category gains share, why (read the posts behind it).
Done when: every number has its evolution and the bullets explain the why, not only the what.
tasks.watch_out: A platform losing share can still be the largest: say both (e.g. Instagram 63% but -20 pts).

tasks.task: Build the brand cluster split slide
tasks.what: Show how the conversation is shared between brand clusters.
tasks.how:
SOV of each cluster in total brand mentions (base 100) and evolution in pts; per country if there are multiple countries within scope.
Add 1 to 2 visuals with verbatims (original + translation) illustrating the growing cluster.
Explain which cluster gains, which one loses, and what it signals for the market.
Done when: the slide states the base ("SOV in total brand mentions, base 100").
tasks.watch_out: The base is brand mentions, not all mentions: posts without any brand are not in this split.

tasks.what: Show category sentiment and what drives it.
tasks.how:
Share of positive, neutral, negative (base 100) with evolution vs P12M in pts and arrows.
For each sentiment, 3 to 5 drivers identified from frequencies and reading (e.g. positive: before / after proof, product launches; neutral: routine content, products as steps; negative: hair loss fear, product disappointment).
1 to 2 verbatims per sentiment, original + translation.
Flag any driver or block below a meaningful volume with the "LOW SIGNAL" tag.
Done when: each driver is supported by verbatims and the legend (% base 100, evolution period, arrow meaning) is on the slide.
tasks.watch_out: Neutral often dominates in categories driven by routine and tutorial content: explain why rather than presenting it as indifference.

tasks.task: Build the market / cultural context slide (if competitive landscape in scope)
tasks.what: Summarize, through the lens of social conversation, how the category works in the market.
tasks.how:
4 blocks, each with 3 bullets and one "Good to know" fact with a figure: e.g. aesthetic codes & proof, authority structure (who consumers trust), identity topics (e.g. textured hair), discovery & trust hierarchy (which creator types are most credible).
Each bullet must come from the corpus or desk research (1.2), not from general knowledge.
Done when: every "Good to know" figure has a source in the working sheet.
tasks.watch_out: Avoid generic market statements that could apply to any country: the slide must say what is specific to THIS market.

tasks.task: Build the top mentioned brands slide
tasks.what: Show the brand ranking in the total category and inside each cluster.
tasks.how:
Top 15 brands by SOV in category brand mentions, with evolution arrows, colored by cluster.
Ranking per cluster (SOV within the cluster), with the hero product of the leaders.
Flag local brands (e.g. country flag) and the client's brand if a brand zoom-in is in scope.
Explain the competitive logic of each cluster (duopoly, one-brand market, open field) and where a challenger has room.
Done when: both rankings use the same brand list and add up correctly.
tasks.watch_out: Check brand and product names against official sources.; The ratio on a base 100 of the top brands should be close to the brand cluster slide (5.3); validate the SOV differences with the analyst.

tasks.task: Build the top rising words and hashtags slide
tasks.what: Show what is emerging in the category conversation.
tasks.how:
From the frequencies (4.5), identify the words and hashtags that over-index in L12M vs P12M (rising words) and the top words overall.
Remove brand names and generic words; group variants and translations.
Explain what drives the main risers (launch, trend, season) with a visual or a verbatim.
Done when: each rising word is clustered into a bigger "what" and explained.
tasks.watch_out: A rising word driven by one viral post is a weak signal: say so.

tasks.what: Compare the category with its benchmark category on the KPIs agreed in 0.3.
tasks.how:
Add the benchmark value next to the category value on the relevant slides (volume growth, platform split, sentiment, topics) or build one comparison slide.
Done when: every benchmark value uses the same period, markets and platforms as the category.

tasks.what: Find the 6 to 8 topics consumers discuss most in the category.
tasks.how:
Standard topics (usually kept): Final results / benefits / efficacy, Skin or hair type /concerns, Formula & ingredients, Scent, Price, Packaging. Texture of the product and formats can be topics depending on the category.
Add, merge or replace topics when the data shows another strong topic or when the brief asks for one; validate with project lead.
Compute the share of each topic (% base 100) and its evolution vs P12M.
Build the overview slide: ranking with share and arrows, one visual per topic, 2 to 3 headline bullets.
Done when: the topic list, volumes and evolutions are validated by the project lead.
tasks.watch_out: The topics are % base 100 of topic mentions: posts can mention several topics, state the base in the footnote.

tasks.what: Explain what consumers say inside each topic and what it means for brands.
tasks.how:
Per topic: one intro slide (topic name + share, 3 insight bullets, one long typical verbatim with translation), then 1 to 2 data slides.
Data slides use the facets of the topic. Examples: Final results: expected results on functionality vs on appearance (base 100), top concerns with a zoom on the most mentioned and fastest growing concern (its causes and top associated brands). Hair / skin type: split by type, semantics and sentiment word clouds, deep dive on the most vocal type. Formula & ingredients: top ingredients by family (actives, proteins, oils, harsh chemicals), trend focus (e.g. skinification actives with what they are used for), chemicals driving negativity, share of naturality / clean claims. Scent, price, packaging: drivers, products mentioned, positive vs negative.
Each data slide: an insight headline, 2 to 3 bullets, charts with base, 2 verbatims (original + translation), source line.
Done when: every topic has its intro and data slides and each insight is traceable to the corpus.
tasks.watch_out: Mark small sub-blocks as "LOW SIGNAL" and marke any cultural specificities in "good to know" boxes in the slide. Do not deep dive a topic with too little volume: fold it into another one.

tasks.task: Identify and size the category personas
tasks.what: Identify the 6 to 8 category personas who drive the conversation.
tasks.how:
Follow the PERSONA methodology document at CATEGORY level: personas are segmented on need / pain point and expertise, not on brand relationship.
Use the facets already built (concerns, hair / skin types, routines, results expected, brand clusters) as the main signals.
Size each persona with one query / facet per persona, base 100, evolution vs P12M; adjust with the qualitative reading and log every adjustment.
Overview slide: all personas with name, visual, share and arrow.
Done when: the persona list and shares are validated by the project lead.
tasks.watch_out: Shares are a split of persona conversations, not of consumers: say it in the footnote.; Make sure the personae's driving motivations/core identity approximately matches with the top topic % if there is an overlap (example: skin concerns are 23% of top topics; then a skin concerns personae cannot be 5%); flag to proejct lead and validate changes in personae facettes

tasks.task: Build the persona ID cards (if requested)
tasks.what: Give one portrait per persona.
tasks.how:
Moodboard slide per persona: visuals + the persona's overindexing hashtags.
ID card per persona, same blocks for all: socio-demographics (generations, gender, inferred from profiles), brand cluster affinity (% per cluster + leading brand), top words & hashtags (word cloud), centers of interest (top 5), who are they (60 to 90 words, singular, "she / he..."), motivations (3), barriers (3 to 4), one verbatim (original + translation).
Done when: every attribute can be traced to posts or profiles read.
tasks.watch_out: Generations and gender are inferred, not measured: never present them as survey data.

tasks.what: Show the brand's conversation compared with the category.
tasks.how:
Same layout as 5.1: brand mentions and evolution, positive share, platform split and sub-category split, each with the category value next to it ("vs 49% Category").
Explain where the brand follows or diverges from the category momentum.
Done when: every brand value has its category comparison.
tasks.watch_out: On a small base (e.g. 1.5K mentions), say it in the headline and avoid over-reading point changes.

tasks.what: Show the brand's sentiment and its drivers vs the category.
tasks.how:
Same layout as 5.3 with the category value under each share; drivers named with the brand's products.
Done when: positive and negative drivers each have product-level verbatims.
tasks.watch_out: Negative sentiment on a small base: use the LOW SIGNAL tag and quote precisely what consumers criticize.

tasks.task: Build the top brands associated slide
tasks.what: Show which brands consumers mention together with the brand, and how it changes.
tasks.how:
Share of brand conversations that mention at least one other brand.
Top 10 associated brands in P12M and in L12M side by side, colored by cluster, flagging "new in top 10" and "no longer in top 10", plus the shift by cluster.
Explain the content formats behind co-mentions (routines, hauls, "TikTok made me buy", favorites of the month).
Done when: both periods use the same base.

tasks.task: Build the territories and values slides (if in scope)
tasks.what: Show the brand's territory footprint and its equity values vs competitors. Validate if needed with project lead & brief
tasks.how:
Territories: brand shares on the territories of 5.6 vs the category, overindex and gaps.
Values: define 5 to 6 brand values from reading (e.g. expertise, support & inclusivity, sustainability & transparency, fearlessness, self-love, trendiness); compare the brand with 5 competitors (% of each brand's conversation carrying the value) with evolution; give the brand's rank per value.
Done when: values are defined in the working sheet and applied identically to all compared brands.
tasks.watch_out: Competitors compared here must be the ones validated in 0.1, using the same facets.

tasks.task: Build the brand top topics slides
tasks.what: Show what consumers discuss about the brand vs the category.
tasks.how:
Same topics as 6.1, with the brand share and the category share for each.
If within scope & brief: Deep dive the topics where the brand overindexes or that the brief targets (intro slide + data slide, as in 6.2), e.g. scent drivers, packaging (emotional vs functional), price acceptance.
Done when: each deep dive explains what is specific to the brand; validate with project lead if deep dives are needed.

tasks.task: Build the correlating audiences slides (if in scope)
tasks.what: Show how the category personas connect with the brand. Validate if needed with project lead & brief
tasks.how:
Share of each category persona in the brand conversation vs in the category; add a brand-specific persona if one appears in reading (labeled "specific to [brand]").
Map the personas to roles for the brand (e.g. awareness driver, conversion driver, advocates, source of recruitment, loyalty / differentiation driver), with shares vs category.
Optional: core fans (audiences who are lovers of the brand) when the brief asks for it.
Done when: shares add up to 100 and the role mapping is validated by the project lead.

tasks.what: Compare the brand's hero products with a direct competitor product on e-commerce reviews.
tasks.how:
Pairs: one hero product of the brand vs one competitor product with the same function (e.g. dry shampoo vs dry shampoo).
Per product: average rating, number of reviews, recommendation rate, product love rate, repurchase intention, sampling rate, each with its evolution and the category average.
Sentiment split of the reviews (negative / neutral / positive).
Top 3 advantages and top 2 disadvantages with their share, compared with the other product; LOW SIGNAL tag where relevant.
Done when: every KPI has the category average and the review count is visible.
tasks.watch_out: A high sampling rate (free / incentivized products) inflates positivity: comment on it when it is far from the category average.

tasks.what: Give the strategic takeaways of the study, section by section. As inspiration for the project lead
tasks.how:
Group the key learnings by deck section (Digital footprint, Market context, Competitive landscape, Topics & audiences, Brand zoom-in, R&R).
Each learning: a numbered headline (one sentence, the "so what") + 2 to 4 lines of evidence with figures from the deck.
Use the Claude skill "sl-insight-creation" to sharpen headlines.
Done when: each learning connects back to the business question and every figure matches the slides.
tasks.watch_out: A key learning that only repeats a slide headline adds nothing: it must link several findings.

tasks.what: Turn the learnings into directions the client can act on. As inspiration for the project lead
tasks.how:
3 to 5 recommendations, each with a short title and 2 to 3 lines linking it to the learnings.
Validate them with the project lead before they go to the client.
Done when: each recommendation is traceable to at least one key learning.
tasks.watch_out: Recommendations are input for the client's strategic reflection: keep them grounded in the data and flag where they go beyond it.

tasks.what: Keep the project team aligned throughout the audit.
tasks.how:
Plan at least 2 to 3 review calls per week with the project team.
Key checkpoints: perimeter and clusters (end of phase 1), final volume (3.6), facets (4.1 and 4.5), topic list (6.1), personas (7.1), storyline before building slides.

tasks.what: Make sure the deck is correct and clean.
tasks.how:
All base 100 splits add up to 100; evolutions use the same periods everywhere (L12M vs P12M).
Every chart states its base; every slide has the source line (platforms + period).
Every verbatim matches the original post (wording, emoji, hashtags), translation re-read by a native speaker, authors anonymized.
Brand, product and retailer names checked; cluster colors consistent; LOW SIGNAL tags in place.
Remove annotations, placeholders, internal notes; do not share queries.
Done when: the all inconcistencies are logged and project lead validates.
tasks.watch_out: After any late change in perimeter, clusters or personas, recheck every split that depends on it.

tasks.what: Close the project and improve the next one.
tasks.how:
Archive queries, facets, brand list and clusters, volumes, decision log and working sheet in the Project Drive (they are the starting point of the next audit, see 0.2).
After the restitution, ask the project lead for written feedback (plus a quick coffee or call if needed).
tasks.watch_out: For recurring clients, keep perimeter, clusters, territories and persona definitions stable between waves so they can be compared.

deck.title: Category Audit | Deck Structure
deck.description: Standard slide sequence of a category audit deck, with the data each slide needs and when it is included.
rows: Category name, market flag(s), date; agenda listing the parts in scope.
Client situation and business question; markets, period, platforms; how the data was collected and analyzed.
One box per cluster: definition (pricing, distribution, purchase driver) and brand logos.
Consumer discussions: split by platform & sub-category
Total mentions + evolution, % positive, platform split with pts, sub-category donut base 100.
Consumer discussions: split by brand cluster
Cluster SOV in brand mentions base 100 with pts, 1 to 2 visuals + verbatims.
Positive / neutral / negative with pts, drivers per sentiment, verbatims, LOW SIGNAL tags, legend.
4 blocks (e.g. aesthetic codes & proof, authority structure, identity, discovery & trust) with Good to know facts.
Share of point-of-sale mentions, split by channel, drivers, top retailers.
6 to 8 territories, SOV total category with growth, shares per cluster, top 3 and overindex (> 2 pts).
Top 15 brands in category, ranking within each cluster, arrows, local flags, hero products.
Risers L12M vs P12M, with explanation.
6 to 8 topics ranked, % base 100 with arrows, visual per topic.
Topic + share, 3 insight bullets, long verbatim + translation.
Topic data slides (1 to 2 per topic)
E.g. results expected (functional vs appearance), concerns + causes zoom, hair / skin type split + semantics, ingredients by family, trend focus, negative chemicals, naturality claims.
6 to 8 personas with name, visual, share, arrow.
Persona moodboard + ID card (x each persona)
Moodboard with hashtags; ID card with socio-demographics, cluster affinity, top words, interests, who are they, motivations, barriers, verbatim.
Same as P1 slide with category values beside each brand value.
Same as P1 sentiment, with category comparison and product-level drivers.
% of brand posts mentioning another brand; top 10 associated P12M vs L12M; new / no longer in top 10.
Territory footprint vs category; values vs 5 competitors with rank.
If brand focus and if requested
Topics vs category; deep dives on overindexed topics.
If brand focus and if requested
Category personas on the brand vs category, brand-specific persona, role mapping; core fans if requested.
If brand focus and if requested
Brand hero vs competitor: rating, reviews, recommendation, love, repurchase, sampling vs category, sentiment, advantages / disadvantages.
If R&R in scope and if requested
Numbered learnings per section: headline + evidence.
